newsitem.title: USA: Los Alamos nuclear lab to submit to emission audit.
newsitem.headline: Los Alamos nuclear lab to submit to emission audit.

text.p: Avoiding potential fines of $2.5 billion, the U.S. Energy Department on Tuesday agreed to allow an outside auditor to monitor radioactive air emissions from the nation's top nuclear weapons laboratory at Los Alamos, New Mexico.

The agreement, which could eventually cost the government about $1.3 million, settled a five-year-old lawsuit by Concerned Citizens for Nuclear Safety. The Santa Fe, New Mexico, group accused the laboratory of violating clean air rules.
The settlement would open a U.S. nuclear weapons facility to a citizen-directed audit for the first time ever.
The government admitted that monitoring systems on 31 out of 33 stacks that emit radioactive particles at Los Alamos National Laboratory failed to meet U.S. Clean Air Act standards from 1991 to 1996.

But a spokesman for Los Alamos said measurements taken around the 43-square-mile site in northern New Mexico showed that emissions from the lab never exceeded federal limits or reached hazardous levels during the five years.
"We maintain there has been no risk to public safety or worker safety," said spokesman John Gustafson.
While not accusing the government of endangering people's health, the citizens' group said the government could not prove it had been in compliance with federal standards.

"They don't have the measurements to demonstrate that," said Arjun Makhijani, president of the Institute of Energy and Environmental Research, which will work with the auditors on behalf of the citizens' group to ensure a thorough monitoring of Los Alamos.
Under the agreement, the government will pay no more than $700,000 in total for a team, approved by the citizens' group, to conduct audits in 1997 and 2000, and, if necessary, again in 2002 and 2003.

"If the auditor finds significant problems, we expect (Los Alamos) to rectify them promptly, or we'll be back in court to see that they do," Carol Oppenheimer, legal counsel for Concerned Citizens for Nuclear Safety, said in a statement.
The government agreed to cover the costs of the Institute for Energy and Environmental Research's work and to give the University of New Mexico $450,000 to set up environmental health courses.
